_about: Hand direction per line, keyed by line ID (a passer-by's two takes share the ID without .m/.f). 'hash' is the hash of the words it was written for; tools/voice/extract.py reports direction left behind by a rewrite. 'say' replaces the voiceable form sent to the TTS.

rook.first.1.pace: brisk, dry, bossy at the end
rook.first.1.wants: to get the stranger sat down and fed
rook.first.1.notes: She already knows who you are (she's paid to know; Vonnra's money is under the 'Well.'). Chid's babbling is a fond eye-roll. 'Sit down before you fall down' is kindness as an order: warm and bossy, no softening.

rook.first.2.wants: to sell a bed and size up a guest
rook.first.2.notes: 'Another one off the Low Ford road' is a note she'll pass to Vonnra later, said lightly. The services rattle off like a counted list; 'if you ask nicely' with a dry twinkle.

rook.hub.1.notes: Three short beats at the end of a long day. 'Beds aren't' is the kindness, said sideways with a breath of a laugh.

rook.hub.2.notes: 'There you are' as if she'd been waiting. 'Don't tell the others' dropped low, a laugh on the out-breath; she'd never call it fondness.

rook.hub.3.notes: Landlady's patter, dry and practised. No warmth spent, none withheld.

rook.rumours.1.pace: brisk gossip, slower on the dog
rook.rumours.1.wants: to pass on the talk, and the one bit that bothers her
rook.rumours.1.notes: 'You did half of it' with a laugh on the out-breath. The counting jokes are quick. The dog whining at the floor is the real news (the knocking under the Penhale farm); let her slow a touch, puzzled, without making it spooky.

rook.rumours.2.wants: to share the good news without fuss
rook.rumours.2.notes: Enjoys Holloway sulking. 'Harlan's still asking after his boy, mind' drops the tone a notch; the 'mind' is her conscience.

rook.rumours.3.pace: brisk, cooler, pause before 'Make of that'
rook.rumours.3.wants: to let them know she's noticed
rook.rumours.3.notes: 'None.' stands alone. The pelts and Maeca's absence are laid out flat as evidence. 'Make of that what you like' is a pointed, dry judgement, never a lecture.

rook.rumours.4.pace: brisk, easy, a grumble at the end
rook.rumours.4.wants: to gossip and collect a debt
rook.rumours.4.notes: 'Which is how you know it's settled' is her dry philosophy, laugh on the out-breath. The Jessop debt is a grumble, but she's flagging it on purpose.

rook.rumours.5.wants: to share a happy house, and the confusion
rook.rumours.5.notes: Pleased about Jory in the good room; Harlan paying twice amuses her. Then the wolves as three competing stories; 'Pick one' is dry and a bit fed-up.

rook.rumours.6.notes: Harlan's shut out even her, which hurts more than she shows. 'I've stopped asking' is tired, not callous; no laugh this time.

rook.rumours.7.pace: brisk, rattling list, a beat before Jessop
rook.rumours.7.wants: to give them the threads to pull
rook.rumours.7.notes: Runs through the wolf stories quickly; then slows slightly to drop Jessop, deliberately. 'Pick a story' is dry; she knows which one she'd pick.

rook.clerk.pace: brisk, then a pause, then grumble
rook.clerk.wants: to point them at Jessop without saying so
rook.clerk.notes: 'Clerks don't buy rounds' is her whole case. 'Rav's always there' is a dry aside with weight. Pause; Jessop missing worries her, so she covers it with the unpaid third round.

rook.town.notes: A speech she's given a hundred times. 'A girl in shiny armour will tell you why, at length' has an affectionate laugh on the out-breath. The last line is a dry warning.

rook.runs.wants: to show she's the one who really knows
rook.runs.notes: Three people, three verbs, each drier. 'And I feed all three of them' lands with quiet pride and a laugh on the breath; she knows more than all of them.

rook.ford.wants: to confess before it's found out
rook.ford.notes: Ordinary at first. Pause, then the admission about Vonnra's money, admitted because she admits most things. 'Don't look like that, pet' brushes it off; don't play it guilty, play it as business with a small unease underneath.

rook.ford2.pace: slow, flat, a beat between each
rook.ford2.notes: The bossiness drains out. 'She's never paid me double for anything' is said to herself as much as to you; the first crack of doubt about Vonnra. No laugh.

rook.firstlamp.pace: unhurried, warmer, firm at the end
rook.firstlamp.wants: to have Ashe left in peace
rook.firstlamp.notes: Town history told with real pride; slows on 'the last one lit'. 'He'd have wanted it used' is generous. 'Just leave him where he lies' is an order, quiet and not negotiable.

rook.c.wants: to work out who C. was
rook.c.notes: Brushes it off, then the pause where it catches. 'Now there's a thing' is quiet interest; she doesn't know her mother's bread went to Chid, but the note tugs at something.

rook.lamp.pace: warm, steady, dry at the end
rook.lamp.notes: Her mother's lamp is the one thing she's sentimental about; keep it under the dryness. 'Lord knows he doesn't' is an affectionate jab at Chid, laugh on the out-breath.

rook.wanted.wants: to keep trouble from her door
rook.wanted.notes: She covered for you and wants you to know it. 'Which is true' is a dry aside. The warning is real, bossy, and fond.

rook.cb_shrine_lit.notes: Chid without his shoes is told fondly. 'My mother's lamp's got a sister again' is the moment she nearly goes; pause, then the free bowl and 'Don't make a habit of it' gruff and quick to cover. Never tearful.

rook.cb_freed_teamsters.notes: A scolding that's really thanks. 'Bringing that much crying into one house' with a laugh on the out-breath.

rook.cb_burned_roost.pace: slow, flat, pause in the middle
rook.cb_burned_roost.wants: to shut them out of her kitchen
rook.cb_burned_roost.notes: No 'pet', no laugh. 'There were people in those cages' is plain and heavy. Pause. She'll take your money (business) but not have you near her; the distinction is the judgement.

rook.cb_nemesis_slain.notes: Bossy approval; the maxim is how she runs her life (and her debts). Firm, a little grim.

rook.cb_opened_vault.notes: Smells it on you; chooses not to ask. 'And get it wrong' is a fond dig at Chid.

rook.say_calling.1.notes: Reads your posture like a ledger. 'Or wanted to be' is gentle needling.

rook.say_calling.2.notes: Warning as a joke at your expense. 'Twice' is the punchline, with the out-breath laugh.

rook.say_calling.3.notes: Half order, half bawdy joke about Sella; said straight-faced.

rook.say_calling.4.wants: to keep tabs on a quiet one
rook.say_calling.4.notes: She doesn't like being surprised in her own house. 'That door always makes a sound' is wary; the bell threat is a fond joke.

rook.say_calling.5.wants: to keep track of who comes in
rook.say_calling.5.notes: Same words, slightly more suspicious: a landlady who must know who's in her house (and report it). The bell is a joke with a point.

rook.say_woman.notes: Matter-of-fact advice from a woman who's seen it. The twist about the wives is dry, almost funny, but she means it.

rook.t_rook.pace: brisk, then slower, a deflection at the end
rook.t_rook.wants: to not admit she misses him
rook.t_rook.notes: Fond list of his faults. 'Went up the north road with the last lot' is a quiet loss. 'It's a good chair; that's the only reason' is the lie: say it firmly, too firmly.

rook.cb_told_brannoc.pace: slow, pause while she wipes the counter
rook.cb_told_brannoc.wants: to do something kind with her hands
rook.cb_told_brannoc.notes: She knew, or guessed, and couldn't tell him. Long pause, wiping the same bit of counter. 'Good.' is quiet. 'It was never going to be me' is an admission. Then the bossy order to sit, which is the comfort; never cries.

holloway.first.1.wants: to get the red off the stranger before trouble starts
holloway.first.1.notes: Anger held one notch below the surface; the threat is plain, not shouted. Hoarse, tired; the cells joke is bitter arithmetic. 'Captain of what's left of the Watch' drops a little: the shame is in 'what's left'.

holloway.first.2.wants: to acknowledge the deed without owing for it
holloway.first.2.notes: 'The Watch kept those lamps, once' is a quiet sore point (he hasn't had oil in years). 'Thanks don't feed eleven men' is the quartermaster: he counts even gratitude. Flat, no warmth to spare.

holloway.first.3.notes: 'At night.' stands alone, suspicious. Weary contempt for both good and lucky. Name and rank are a formality, barked low; hoarse from shouting.

holloway.hub.1.pace: dry, slower, a dry turn at the end
holloway.hub.1.wants: to admit a mistake without losing face
holloway.hub.1.notes: 'I was wrong about them' costs him; say it plainly, not humbly. 'Don't tell anyone I said so' is the nearest he comes to a joke: dry, unsmiling.

holloway.hub.2.pace: clipped list, then slower, then back to business
holloway.hub.2.wants: to keep counting so he doesn't feel it
holloway.hub.2.notes: He lists Aldo like a muster roll: wife, knee, humming. 'They took him off it by the bad leg' is one plain line, no dwelling. 'I'd give a month's pay' is how he grieves: in money. Then he snaps back to five a pelt, too quickly.

holloway.hub.3.notes: He's just turned Sallow's silver-sealed letter face down and put his cup on it. 'What.' is not a question: a closed door, quiet and a beat too quick.

holloway.hub.4.wants: to keep them at arm's length
holloway.hub.4.notes: No shouting; the danger is how quiet it is. Each word an order.

holloway.hub.5.notes: He straightened when you came in, and resents it. 'You.' slightly gruffer to cover; 'What is it?' brisk.

holloway.hub.6.wants: to keep the killer at a distance
holloway.hub.6.notes: The fever year is a dark yardstick. 'Try not to put any down in my square' is dry, but he means it.

holloway.hub.7.notes: 'I paid for every pelt of it' is a quartermaster's guilt. The question is rhetorical; then Maeca, and his voice goes quieter, as it always does on her name.

holloway.hub.8.notes: Numbers that don't add up anger him. Drop in volume on 'Maeca's right'; 'and I hate that' is honest, almost rueful. Then the snap back to 'What is it?'.

holloway.hub.9.wants: to get back to the count
holloway.hub.9.notes: A quartermaster's excuse that's also true. Hoarse and short.

holloway.wolves.wants: to get real results, not tales
holloway.wolves.notes: Numbers first: five, fifty, eleven, four. Lean on 'proof' (never 'evidence'). 'Four of them can hold a spear the right way round' is bitter arithmetic, no laugh. Anger one notch down.

holloway.maeca.wants: to not say what she never got
holloway.maeca.notes: He goes very quiet when Maeca comes up. 'She's earned that' is respect. Long pause. '...She's earned a lot of things she never got' is the boots, unsaid: barely above a murmur, eyes elsewhere.

holloway.ashford.pace: very quiet, slow, then abruptly brisk
holloway.ashford.wants: to close the subject before it opens
holloway.ashford.notes: Ashford: his voice goes almost to nothing. 'I counted boots... and I was good at it' is the confession he can't make, said as a boast that curdles. 'That's all you're getting' firm and low; 'Something else?' too quick, a door slammed softly.

holloway.bounty.1.notes: Real respect for the old wolf in 'the old devil himself'. Pays promptly: his version of honour. 'And my thanks with it' is rare and brief.

holloway.bounty.2.notes: Quartermaster mode: almost relieved to have something to count.

holloway.liar.pace: clipped, building, then cold and level
holloway.liar.wants: to make the liar answer for it
holloway.liar.notes: Quotes 'dealt with' back with contempt. The drover is plain fact. 'So.' is a held breath. He swears rarely and here it lands: 'fucking' cold and deliberate, not shouted.

holloway.repaid.notes: Wry; for him paying is the nearest thing to sorry, and he respects it in others. 'I've written both halves down' is a ledger-keeper's warning, not a threat.

holloway.argued.notes: The '...' is him thinking it through. The bucket image is quartermaster logic; 'we'll call it square' is a deal offered, not forgiveness.

holloway.defied.notes: Never shouts; the menace is in the detail. 'Out of my sight' hard and flat; the cell-rats line deliberately ugly and quiet.

holloway.caravan.pace: clipped, factual, hard at the end
holloway.caravan.wants: to make it clear the Watch did its job
holloway.caravan.notes: His men were on the road; it's a point of pride and of duty. 'And whoever told them otherwise lied' lands hard: he suspects a bought clerk.

holloway.caravan2.wants: to not have to name names
holloway.caravan2.notes: He's reasoning like a quartermaster: who knew the manifest. 'I don't like a single name on it' is quiet; he knows these people.

holloway.sick.pace: flat, then a beat, then considered
holloway.sick.wants: to spend less money on wolves
holloway.sick.notes: First line a soldier's shrug. The pause is him doing the sums. The second half is pragmatic, not converted: paying for pelts till he's old is a weary picture.

holloway.cause.1.wants: to stop paying for the wrong thing
holloway.cause.1.notes: 'Of course it's the lamplings' is exasperated, not surprised. 'I'll not pay men to put down sick dogs' is decency stated as accounting. Decisive.

holloway.cause.2.wants: to make a deal and keep his guard
holloway.cause.2.notes: Same exasperation, less conviction: he'll stop the bounty, not his watch. 'I won't stop watching the road' is stubborn, flat.

holloway.lie.wants: to believe it, and not quite
holloway.lie.notes: Wants it to be true; pays. 'I'll grant you that' is cautious. The last line is a dry warning he hopes he won't need.

holloway.expose.1.pace: clipped list, a bite on Pell, then dry
holloway.expose.1.notes: Reads the ledger like an audit: 'R.' then Jessop then 'On the night.' 'You careful, greedy little man' is contempt said almost with relish. Pause; the strongbox pardon is grudging and dry: 'Once.' is the warning.

holloway.expose.2.pace: clipped list, then slower and plain
holloway.expose.2.wants: to pay what he owes, in words for once
holloway.expose.2.notes: Audit voice through the names; bite on 'careful, greedy little man'. Then the turn: 'The Watch owes you' is rare and costly. 'I've not much to pay you with' is the truth of the unpaid Watch, said plainly.

holloway.arrest.wants: to settle it without a fight
holloway.arrest.notes: A quartermaster setting a fine: the price stated, the alternative stated. Tired of trouble, not cruel.

holloway.cb_killed_greymuzzle.1.notes: He'd stopped the bounty; this was done for no pay, and that disturbs him more than a mercenary. 'I'm trying to work out what that makes you' is quiet and watchful.

holloway.cb_killed_greymuzzle.2.wants: to make sense of an odd grief
holloway.cb_killed_greymuzzle.2.notes: Maeca's silence is a dry joke, but her name still drops his voice. Pause. 'Twenty years' and 'odd, missing a thing you hated' are quieter, almost wondering.

holloway.cb_burned_roost.wants: to let the survivor know he knows
holloway.cb_burned_roost.notes: Ashford's people were in those cages; he won't say it. 'I've hanged men for less' flat and heavy. The last sentence is deliberate, every clause measured; anger one notch under, held there with effort.

holloway.cb_freed_teamsters.notes: 'Thin as rakes and alive' has real feeling under it. The put-down about his own men is self-deprecating, dry; he's proud of you and won't say so.

holloway.cb_tricked_redcowl.notes: Starts stern. 'The Watch was in bed' deadpan. Then he argues with himself: 'But it worked. Did it work? It worked.' quickening, almost a laugh he won't allow.

holloway.cb_opened_vault.wants: to know what's below his town
holloway.cb_opened_vault.notes: Duty and history first, then 'I'm too tired' as a confession. The question is genuine and a little afraid.

holloway.cb_vault2.notes: 'Course it is' heavy and unsurprised. He has enough to count; another weight he refuses.

holloway.cb_nemesis_slain.notes: A soldier's compliment about boots (his old trade); a faint sting in the word.

holloway.cb_core_stolen.notes: He'd rather not hear the answer; quiet, watchful, almost resigned.

holloway.say_calling.1.notes: A flicker of hope; pause; he does the sums. 'I can't afford you either way' is dry and a bit sad: his men unpaid a year.

holloway.say_calling.2.notes: A measured warning; 'both sides of a gate' from experience. Not hostile, watchful.

holloway.say_calling.3.wants: to keep fire off his walls
holloway.say_calling.3.notes: The barracks roof is a dry, exasperated anecdote. The order at the end firm.

holloway.say_calling.4.notes: One professional to another. 'One of us should be paid for it' is a tired joke about his unpaid post.

holloway.say_calling.5.notes: Same words, slightly cooler and more watchful; still the tired pay joke at the end.

holloway.say_woman.pace: measured, beat before the last clause
holloway.say_woman.notes: Corrects himself mid-thought. The dead men are said plainly. 'It's no place' is flat and fair: a warning for anyone.

holloway.t_holloway.pace: slow, list, a beat before the dog
holloway.t_holloway.wants: to let a little of himself out
holloway.t_holloway.notes: The list is quartermaster style, in order of priority. Pause; 'Don't tell the men about the dog' is shy, the softest he gets; almost a smile.

holloway.ledger_early.pace: slow read, then clipped, then very quiet
holloway.ledger_early.wants: to not have to act yet
holloway.ledger_early.notes: He reads it twice, standing then sitting. The figures are read like an audit; 'that's the night' lands heavy. Shuts the book. 'Don't tell me where you got it' is low and deliberate: he can't afford to know.

holloway.ledger_early2.pace: clipped, wry, quieter at the end
holloway.ledger_early2.wants: to keep his hands clean until there's proof
holloway.ledger_early2.notes: He wants Pell; he needs proof. 'More thieves than letters' is a tired joke. The Low Kiln man is a real fear. 'Keep it somewhere I can't see it' is half order, half plea.

holloway.post.notes: A long silence before he speaks. The description as recognition; '...Corran.' lands like a name off a roll. He wrote two men down as deserters; the guilt is in how flatly he says it. Very quiet.

holloway.post2.pace: slow, measured, a pause after the writing
holloway.post2.wants: to bury Corran properly, and find who lit the lamps
holloway.post2.notes: Oil is supply, his trade: he knows who hasn't had it. He writes something and crosses it out: pause. 'So somebody had oil. And a reason.' quiet suspicion. 'An apology he can't hear' is as close to sorry as he ever gets; nearly inaudible.

holloway.letter.notes: The letter is Sallow asking for you; he won't let you near it. 'Mine.' is a wall. The cup doesn't move during the pause. Last line is a quiet warning dressed as dry wit.

maeca.first.1.wants: to find out if this one sees what she sees
maeca.first.1.notes: A hunter's half-voice, reading your walk like tracks. 'They're running' is the point she's waited to say to someone who'd understand. 'Barefoot, before you ask' is dry, heading off the usual question.

maeca.first.2.wants: to make the stranger feel the skins they're wearing
maeca.first.2.notes: Contempt kept quiet and final; she never raises her voice. 'And so can they' is the warning. 'What do you want?' is flat, not curious.

maeca.first.3.pace: level, even, drop at the end
maeca.first.3.notes: Disdain for Holloway's bounty, said low. The turn is 'of the Ashford garrison': a breath, then 'What's left of it' almost under the voice; that's all she'll ever give of Ashford unasked.

maeca.hub.1.wants: to be left with her drink, but hear it
maeca.hub.1.notes: She doesn't look up from her cup. Two flat sentences; not unwelcoming, just spent.

maeca.hub.2.wants: to hear the news from someone she trusts
maeca.hub.2.notes: Calling you 'Hunter' is her highest regard. A small lift of real interest on the question; no smile.

maeca.hub.3.notes: Not hostile; she simply hasn't decided about you. Even and dry.

maeca.driving.pace: level, a little faster through the list
maeca.driving.wants: to get someone to look into it
maeca.driving.notes: Present-tense fieldcraft: deer thin, Pack thinner. She's fond of Greymuzzle and won't show it; 'more than a hundred pelts' is a dig at bounty-hunters. Soften slightly on Tam; she's one of the few who believes him.

maeca.tracks.notes: 'You saw that? Nobody sees that.' is genuine surprise, the first respect. Then the diagnosis, steady. 'So. Not bold. Sick.' falls as three short, settled steps.

maeca.truth.pace: level, firm, eases at the end
maeca.truth.notes: 'Should've known' is anger at herself and the Dig, kept low. The instruction is plain. The last two lines soften: relief that the Pack can come back, said as a hunter's forecast, not hope.

maeca.speak.wants: to keep the survivor alive in the Hollow
maeca.speak.notes: Instructions as if teaching a child to cross ice. Respect for Greymuzzle in 'isn't stupid'. 'If he decides wrong, well.' A beat, then 'Run then.' bone-dry, the nearest she gets to a joke.

maeca.where.wants: to be findable, on her terms
maeca.where.notes: The most relaxed she gets. 'Fool enough' is self-mockery; 'drinking Rav's piss' is a flat, earthy joke, no laugh. Keep the half-voice.

maeca.barefoot.notes: The boots are the wound under everything (Holloway signed for them; she doesn't know it). First two sentences flat and final; a pause; then the hard-won peace of 'I prefer it now'. Never self-pitying.

maeca.signed.notes: 'A good hand and a ledger' is quiet, final contempt for a clerk she's never named. Pause; then she turns it on you, cool and level, a door shut.

maeca.thanks.pace: slow, soft, long pause before thanks
maeca.thanks.wants: to say a thing she's never said
maeca.thanks.notes: Reports the Hollow like a weather check, then the admission that she has never saved anything; it costs her. A long pause, and 'Thank you' almost in the half-voice, plain, no tremble.

maeca.cold.notes: She never raises her voice; that's what makes it hurt. 'I heard.' is flat; the line about Holloway's gold is ice, not sarcasm.

maeca.gone.1.notes: Her lover killed Greymuzzle, the wolf that saved her. Three short statements with weight on 'after I told you'. Voice stays low and level; the hardness is in the stops, not volume.

maeca.gone.2.notes: Three fragments, then the dismissal. Quiet and final; grief for Greymuzzle under the ice.

maeca.cb_burned_roost.pace: level, slow, very quiet at the end
maeca.cb_burned_roost.wants: to make the survivor know what they did
maeca.cb_burned_roost.notes: Those cages held her old neighbours. 'I know what fire does in a ravine' is close to the bone; 'I was at Ashford' is three words, the limit she allows herself, barely voiced.

maeca.say_calling.1.wants: to keep them from being torn
maeca.say_calling.1.notes: Approval, then fieldcraft. 'A raised arm's a raised arm' is plain wolf logic; no lecture.

maeca.say_calling.2.notes: Practical, about smell and iron. A slight edge on 'that's been used': she knows what that blade's done.

maeca.say_calling.3.pace: slower, low on the last line
maeca.say_calling.3.wants: to keep fire out of the Hollow
maeca.say_calling.3.notes: 'Fire's the one thing they all remember' carries Ashford under it (fire in the ravine) without saying so. Lower and quieter on the end.

maeca.say_calling.4.notes: Respect for quiet feet; then the pause, and 'Pity about the boots' as a dry jab with the whole history of boots underneath it.

maeca.say_calling.5.notes: Same words as the stalker take, a touch more distant: a compliment, a pause, a dry little jab. The boots carry her secret; don't lean on it.

maeca.invite.wants: to have company without asking for it
maeca.invite.notes: She finishes her cup and stands. An invitation dressed as a dare; 'Most can't' is teasing in the flattest possible way. Don't warm it up, the warmth is that she's asking at all.

maeca.blind.1.wants: to hold the place of a scene not yet written
maeca.blind.1.notes: Writer's placeholder, not for recording; if a guide take is needed, read it flat and low as a stage note, not as prose.

maeca.blind.2.wants: to let trust arrive without anyone naming it
maeca.blind.2.notes: Low and close, as if not to wake her. Let the last clause, 'and the other on you', settle with no smile pushed into it.

maeca.blind_morning.1.wants: to keep the morning a little longer
maeca.blind_morning.1.notes: Grey light, barefoot in the frost, listening. She's told you Ashford already and is lighter for it. 'He'll count us both' is a fond, dry joke at Holloway; a near-smile in the voice.

maeca.blind_morning.2.wants: to tell it once and never again
maeca.blind_morning.2.notes: The one time she talks about Ashford: plain and present, the hunter's half-voice. Hold on 'Kept everything off'; then '...That's why' as if closing a gate. 'Don't make it a story' is a guarded plea, not a rebuke.

maeca.cb_broke_promise.notes: Three plain statements of what you did, each colder. Long pause. The last line is final and quiet; she is choosing not to say worse.

maeca.t_maeca.notes: The garrison hunted men; she says it like a fact about deer. 'Men are easier' is chilling because she isn't trying to be.

maeca.kerchiefs.notes: 'Some.' then she drinks and looks at the cup. 'Fed some of them, once. Buried more.' is as near as she goes; '...Ask me about wolves' is the door shut, quiet, not rude.

wenna.first.1.wants: to keep a scholar's hands off her shelves
wenna.first.1.notes: Clocks the lens and the squint in one glance and enjoys being rude about it. 'You'll only want to catalogue it' is a fond insult. 'What d'you want?' snaps shut.

wenna.first.2.wants: to protect her stock from a stranger
wenna.first.2.notes: Following your hands round the shop: 'Or— yes, that too' breaks off mid-thought. Then the dry boast about things that stop you dying, 'and a few that don't' with a wicked little lilt.

wenna.hub.1.notes: Orders and cancels herself in one breath. 'The stream's clean, child. Clean.' is the payoff: the second 'Clean' slower, almost fierce, relief she would never call relief.

wenna.hub.2.wants: to get back to the pot
wenna.hub.2.notes: Not unkind, just busy. 'Well?' is a prod; the roots are her excuse and her priority.

wenna.animals.pace: brisk, then quickening into the errand
wenna.animals.notes: 'Never.' stands alone, hard: she's seen bad years and won't say which. The metal and smoke frighten her more than she lets on. Speeds up as the practical plan takes over: above the blight if you can, below if you must.

wenna.tamsays.pace: quick, then slows on the admission
wenna.tamsays.wants: to confirm what she's been smelling
wenna.tamsays.notes: Defends Tam brusquely. 'Not fought, not starved: drank.' is the herbalist's diagnosis, hard on 'drank'. Pause. The last line is the closest she comes to fear: she's been telling herself she was old. Keep it dry.

wenna.analyse.1.pace: accelerating, a dash where she catches it
wenna.analyse.1.notes: Starts methodical and then '— what's this? From a pipe?' as she gets interested and speeds up. 'Ember.' lands like a stone; the fever smell is under it. The last two sentences are cold accusation.

wenna.analyse.2.wants: to name the poison and the culprit
wenna.analyse.2.notes: Three sense words, measured: green, warm, chapel lamp (she knows that smell from the fever year). Then the diagnosis at her normal clip. 'Nobody spills this much by accident' is an accusation; she's suspected the ground for a decade.

wenna.analyse_arcana.notes: Rare approval for a fellow expert, then speeds up as she gets into it; the dash before 'ember' is her catching it. Ends on cold certainty about Grimtunnel.

wenna.who.wants: to send them to the pipe safely
wenna.who.notes: Rhetorical questions fired off, not asked. Then instructions like a prescription. 'Especially not if it's clear' is the old-nurse warning, slower and darker.

wenna.root.notes: 'Fat ones, too' is real pleasure she hides in impatience. Rude-kind: payment, then an order.

wenna.mask.pace: brisk, with a catch on 'fever year'
wenna.mask.wants: to hand on the mask and not the memory
wenna.mask.notes: She speaks of the mask as kit and won't name the fever year's dead. 'I'm too old to go where it's needed' is a brave lie (she'd go); play it as a shrug. No sentiment.

wenna.fever.pace: slower than usual, then snaps back to brisk
wenna.fever.notes: The only time she slows right down. Half the valley coughing green: plain, no names. 'Same smell exactly' is the fear she won't admit. Pause, then '...I've roots on the boil' as a hard deflection, back to speed.

wenna.cb_sold_dig.pace: clipped, building, nasty pleasure at the end
wenna.cb_sold_dig.notes: A list of what was sold, with contempt on 'for forty'. 'I tested that water for you, child' is the hurt underneath. The pause, then her spite becomes almost gleeful: very rude, still serving you.

wenna.cb_broke_pump.wants: to be believed about her nose
wenna.cb_broke_pump.notes: Glad, and won't admit it's glad; she pre-empts any doubt. 'Don't argue; I can' is mock-fierce.

wenna.cb_shrine_lit.pace: brisk, a smile at the end
wenna.cb_shrine_lit.notes: The detail of the shoes is her tenderness for Chid, delivered as a complaint. Let a dry chuckle sit behind 'wrong feet'.

wenna.say_calling.1.wants: to get a green thing into them
wenna.say_calling.1.notes: A nurse's diagnosis as an insult. 'Don't lie; I can see your gums' is a sharp, kind jab.

wenna.say_calling.2.notes: Diagnosis, then 'Twice.' with disgust at the bonesetter. 'Sit, I'll— no, you won't sit' breaks off; 'Fine. Limp, then.' is a huff that means she cares.

wenna.say_calling.3.wants: to keep fire off her racks
wenna.say_calling.3.notes: 'Spark-hands' is a disrespectful nickname she enjoys. Speeds up into the anecdote; 'like a funeral for a week' dry and pleased with itself.

wenna.say_calling.4.notes: A diagnosis by look; then commands. 'Don't ask what it is' with a hint of mischief.

wenna.say_calling.5.notes: Same as the stalker take, a touch more grandmotherly. Rude on the surface, a kindness in the hand-off.

wenna.say_woman.wants: to make sure she knows the help is there
wenna.say_woman.notes: Said quietly, no fuss, woman to woman. 'I don't ask which, and I don't tell Chid' is discretion and a little wink at the priest. No sentiment.

wenna.t_wenna.wants: to deflect the question with a joke
wenna.t_wenna.notes: A practised story told quick. The punchline is half true: there's a real loss under 'the best of them'; let it flicker before the joke about the man who won him.

tam.first.pace: rushed, then small at the question
tam.first.notes: Out in one breath, the exact thing he saw. 'Nobody believes me' is hurt, not sulky. Pause; '...You believe me?' is small and open, a nine-year-old's hope.

tam.story.wants: to tell it right, in order
tam.story.notes: Every detail in the order he saw it, landmarks first (the goat fence). The milky eyes 'like Gran's' are the scary bit, slowed just slightly. 'I stayed in town' is proud obedience.

tam.farm.notes: Proud on 'Penhale's, that's us'. Repeats Pa's saying in Pa's gruff cadence, then his own small doubt: 'But these ones aren't right.'

tam.again.1.wants: to be told it'll be all right
tam.again.1.notes: Very short sentences, unlike him; he's scared. 'Not ever, maybe' is said quietly, testing whether it's true.

tam.again.2.notes: Relief Pa's alive, then a nine-year-old's outrage: 'I SAID' is loud, stamped, and then 'Weeks ago' sulky-proud. Never sarcastic.

tam.again.3.pace: run-on, tumbling, delighted at the end
tam.again.3.notes: The hens are a tragedy for one second; then the thrill of Pa calling you a bad word. 'He was smiling, though' is earnest reassurance, a grin in the voice.

tam.again.4.notes: No run-on: the brevity is the fear. 'He always comes in' is a child repeating the rule the world is supposed to follow. Very quiet, not crying.

tam.again.5.notes: A straight question, lifting at the end; he trusts you to have found out.

tam.fetch.wants: to let the small rescue land as a joke the boy's Pa won't share
tam.fetch.notes: Plain fireside telling; the faintest dryness on 'one of them is a fool'. 'He comes.' stands alone, full stop.

tam.happy.notes: Bursting, every sentence an exclamation. 'Did you do it?' is pure earnest wonder, hoping the answer's yes.

tam.cb_killed_greymuzzle.pace: slow, pause before the second question
tam.cb_killed_greymuzzle.notes: Not accusing; he genuinely wants to know. The pause is him working out that a sick wolf isn't a bad wolf. Small voice on '...Was he sick too?'.

tam.cb_grey2.notes: 'Oh.' and a pause while he takes it in. Repeats Pa's rule; 'Pa says a lot of things' is the first doubt in Pa, said earnestly, not cheekily.

tam.t_tam.pace: run-on, sweet, slowing at the end
tam.t_tam.wants: to believe the goat's all right
tam.t_tam.notes: Delighted by the hat. Then he quietly overrules Pa with his own better story. 'I think she's happy' is soft and certain: a child deciding.

tam.tock.pace: one long run-on, breathless, 'tock' clear and even
tam.tock.wants: to make someone believe him about the knocking
tam.tock.notes: One breath of 'and's. Say 'tock' and 'tock' like the sound itself, spaced. 'Moles don't knock' is his logic, firm. 'But it kept knocking' trails off scared; he is right, and nobody knows it yet.

brannoc.first.1.wants: to know if this one's worth his time
brannoc.first.1.notes: 'Hunter. Good.' is the warmest he gets with a stranger: a nod in the voice, no smile. Name and trade are two dropped weights; the hammer is between every phrase.

brannoc.first.2.notes: Three plain statements like strikes on the anvil, then 'Which?' as the only lift. No welcome; he isn't unfriendly, he just doesn't spend words.

brannoc.hub.1.wants: to be let alone with the fire
brannoc.hub.1.notes: Night: the forge is down and so is he. Not a rebuke; a fact about the coals. Keep it deep and quiet, almost under the breath.

brannoc.hub.2.pace: slow, steady, in rhythm with work
brannoc.hub.2.wants: to keep working with company near
brannoc.hub.2.notes: Nell is buried; he keeps hammering while you're there and doesn't send you away, which is new. Say it on the swing of the hammer, plain, with a trace of something like ease.

brannoc.hub.3.pace: slow, two beats then the question
brannoc.hub.3.wants: to show he's glad, without saying it
brannoc.hub.3.notes: 'Back. Good.' is as close as he gets to welcome; let 'Good' sit for a beat before the business question. No smile in the voice, just less weight.

brannoc.hub.4.notes: Three words between hammer strikes. Not cold; this is simply how he says hello.

brannoc.cloak.pace: measured, a touch slower on the end
brannoc.cloak.notes: Pride in the pelts, said flat. The last line is half warning, half satisfaction: every wolf will know it. Don't sell it; let the weight carry it.

brannoc.irons.1.wants: to have the buyer face him
brannoc.irons.1.notes: He now knows what the irons did to Nell. Long silence first (he stares at the rack); the count is recited like a charge sheet. 'Buyer can come and ask me' is a threat in a level voice; never raise it.

brannoc.irons.2.pace: slow, factual, stops before the end
brannoc.irons.2.wants: to account for the stock, and not think about it
brannoc.irons.2.notes: Inventory voice until 'Didn't ask who.' Then a pause and '...Should've' lands as the first crack of guilt; keep it quieter, almost to himself.

brannoc.cb_killed_greymuzzle.notes: Mourns the fang, not the wolf, or says he does. A smith's eye on a trophy; a tiny edge of reproach that it didn't come to him.

brannoc.cb_wolf_slaughter.wants: to mark what it cost the wood
brannoc.cb_wolf_slaughter.notes: Three fragments like three hammer strikes. 'Wood'll be quiet' is not praise; let it sit uneasy, a man who knows what quiet means.

brannoc.say_calling.1.notes: He's looked at your gear without asking. 'No charge for looking' is his kindness, said like a price list. No warmth on the surface.

brannoc.say_calling.2.notes: 'You hit things' is an observation; 'Good.' is the compliment. Tiny lift on 'Good', nothing more.

brannoc.say_calling.3.wants: to find the bit of iron he can fix
brannoc.say_calling.3.notes: Dismisses the staff (not his trade), then the pause where his eye finds the metal. 'That is' (that is my trade) lands with quiet satisfaction.

brannoc.say_calling.4.notes: Each word is a judgement, as if testing each knife's edge with his thumb. Even full stops; no music.

brannoc.say_calling.5.notes: Fallback read of the same line: an appraisal, word by word, as if weighing each blade in the hand. Keep the stops square.

brannoc.t_brannoc.notes: The longest he talks about family. 'Worse temper' has the ghost of a smile; 'Hammer's hers' is reverent and final. Under it, his own daughter, unsaid.

brannoc.mark.1.pace: very slow, long hold between the two words
brannoc.mark.1.wants: to not believe what's in his hand
brannoc.mark.1.notes: He knows Nell's fate; this is his iron from the Warden that killed her. First 'Mine' is recognition; a long silence holding it; the second 'Mine' is near breaking and almost voiceless. Nothing else.

brannoc.mark.2.notes: Identifies his mark plainly, recites the order like a ledger; a beat as he hands it back. 'It's done what it was for' is darker than he knows; say it flat, a door shutting.

brannoc.irons_after.pace: slow, heavy, pause on the hammer
brannoc.irons_after.wants: to wait for the buyer, and know them
brannoc.irons_after.notes: Hand flat on the irons; 'Or herself' is him already suspecting a woman (Vonnra), dry and deliberate. The hammer falls in the pause, then 'I'll know the coin' quiet and absolute.

brannoc.nell.pace: slow, in hammer rhythm, then stops
brannoc.nell.notes: He keeps hammering through the description, a list he's rehearsed: twelve, red hair, new boots. The hammer stops before 'Mine. Nell.', which drops to near nothing. 'You pass them?' is the only question he ever asks; it should cost him.

brannoc.nell_ditch.1.wants: to keep her alive a moment longer
brannoc.nell_ditch.1.notes: He has already put the iron and the ford together. Hammer down, eyes on nothing; he talks about her stubbornness to avoid the fact. The repeated 'reins' softens each time; no crying.

brannoc.nell_ditch.2.wants: to hold on to the girl, not the body
brannoc.nell_ditch.2.notes: He has put the hammer down, which he never does. 'Had the reins' is barely out; a long breath through the nose; then the fond, stubborn memory. Grief held by the jaw, not the voice.

brannoc.nell_gone.notes: 'Water's quick' is him comforting himself. Pause: he holds the hammer and doesn't strike. 'Forge is shut. Go on.' is a dismissal without anger; the door closing on grief.

brannoc.nell_risen.pace: slow, weighed, pause before the question
brannoc.nell_risen.notes: He looks at you properly for the first time. 'Got up' is weighed like an edge; the repeat accepts it. '...Was it quick?' is the hardest thing he will ever ask: very quiet, not pleading.

brannoc.nell_quick.wants: to thank the one who ended it
brannoc.nell_quick.notes: His one 'thank you' in the whole game: after a long silence, low, almost not voiced, and never repeated. Then the forge ticks; 'Forge is shut. Go on.' is gentle for him.

brannoc.nell_slow.notes: He nods as if told a price; takes the blow without a sound. Two words, flat and dead, the forge closing; no anger at you.

brannoc.nell_lie.notes: The hammer comes down between phrases, relieved, almost light. 'She's thin' is a father's fondness; play it straight, so the listener feels the lie he's been told.

brannoc.nell_look.notes: He takes it as a no. The hammer falls; 'No.' to himself; '...Nobody looks' is quiet contempt for the world, not you, and a fear he won't name.

harlan.first.1.pace: tumbling patter, then slows for the name
harlan.first.1.wants: to thank the one who saved Jory before he can say anything else
harlan.first.1.notes: Laughing at Jory's retelling with tears just behind it; the pause is where he takes the survivor's hand in both of his. The last sentence is a little embarrassed at himself, the salesman forgetting his own pitch.

harlan.first.2.pace: flat, slow, long gap before the last line
harlan.first.2.wants: to be left alone without being rude
harlan.first.2.notes: The patter is gone; he does not get up. 'Everyone's heard' is bitter at the town, not the survivor. The trailing pause is him failing to find the salesman, so 'Buy something, or don't' comes out dead.

harlan.first.3.pace: breaks off, rushes, questions tumble faster
harlan.first.3.wants: to know whether Jory is alive
harlan.first.3.notes: The dash is him seeing his seal; the pause is him rounding the counter and not daring to touch it. Three questions, each closer to the one he means; the last, about 'the boy', nearly cracks.

harlan.first.4.wants: to hear that someone has seen the wagons
harlan.first.4.notes: He starts with the trade list out of habit and the 'friend' and boot-sniffing are real merchant charm; the Verge on the survivor's boots makes him hopeful. 'Tell me you've seen something' is almost a plea; lean on 'tell me'.

harlan.first.5.wants: to make the stranger care about Jory
harlan.first.5.notes: A pitch he has given too many times; the crack comes on 'He's never been a week late in his life'. Pause, then the apology is self-aware and a little ashamed.

harlan.first.6.pace: brisk patter that slows on the count
harlan.first.6.notes: Same pitch as yesterday but heavier; 'Six days' lands as a figure he has been counting all night. Stops dead after 'six days late', then apologises.

harlan.first.7.pace: warm patter, a hitch, then the apology
harlan.first.7.wants: to sell himself on the idea that the boy is merely late
harlan.first.7.notes: Earliest and lightest version: he still half-believes it is a delay. Let 'Five days' sound like a merchant reading a ledger, then the pause shows it is not.

harlan.first.8.pace: eager question, then talks himself down
harlan.first.8.wants: to hear the survivor passed the wagons
harlan.first.8.notes: The question jumps out too eagerly; he answers it himself before the survivor can ('No. No, of course you didn't'). The repeated no is him swallowing hope. 'Four days' is the crack.

harlan.hub.1.wants: to share the joy of Jory being home
harlan.hub.1.notes: Proud-uncle exasperation on 'Pretending!', a laugh in it. Under it is relief so big he keeps it light; then straight to business with 'friend'.

harlan.hub.2.pace: repeats, slow, long pause, then clipped
harlan.hub.2.notes: 'I heard. I heard.' is him stopping the survivor speaking. The pause before Holloway's detail; the supper memory nearly breaks him, so he cuts it off and turns brusque on 'What do you want?'

harlan.hub.3.wants: to pretend he has given up hoping
harlan.hub.3.notes: He stays seated. 'I told myself' admits the lie. He asks 'Any word?' and answers 'No' before the survivor can, so it does not hurt to hear it; let a tiny breath go before 'There never is'.

harlan.hub.4.wants: to have the road give Jory back
harlan.hub.4.notes: Spoken while staring at the bend in the road, not at the survivor; half to himself. A faint smile at the picture of Jory shouting, then 'Any word?' turned back without hope.

harlan.hub.5.notes: No patter left; two short questions, the second smaller and more naked than the first.

harlan.what.pace: fast list, then slows on the boy
harlan.what.wants: to be sure the survivor knows what Jory is worth to him
harlan.what.notes: The money talk is easy salesmanship until 'The boy'; there the merchant drops away. 'I'll pay what you ask' is a blank cheque, meant. He blames the wolves because it is the comfortable story.

harlan.route.1.wants: to give every fact that might help
harlan.route.1.notes: He has recited this route to everyone; plain directions in merchant order. 'Nobody saw them' drops in pitch: the part that frightens him.

harlan.route.2.pace: steady recital, a beat before the end
harlan.route.2.notes: Six days back is a number he counts; keep it businesslike so the last line, 'Nobody saw them', lands quiet and heavy.

harlan.route.3.notes: A merchant giving a route; under it, five days of not sleeping. Small catch on 'Vonnra's gate at dusk'.

harlan.route.4.wants: to point the survivor down the right road
harlan.route.4.notes: Earliest version; still believes in finding them. Brisk, helpful, and the 'Nobody saw them' is puzzled more than afraid.

harlan.notwolves.wants: to have someone else find out who
harlan.notwolves.notes: Two broken starts: disbelief, then 'Who—' and he stops himself, because he half suspects why someone would want his wagons. 'Please' is quiet and unsalesman-like.

harlan.jory.wants: to give the survivor everything at once
harlan.jory.notes: 'Alive' twice, the second a near-shout with a sob in it; the dash is him fumbling the purse. 'Cost!' is the merchant's highest praise; 'Don't tell anyone' is a wet, conspiratorial laugh.

harlan.box.notes: Honest gratitude with a salesman's flourish; he is also relieved what is inside stayed unopened, so the 'Unopened' is a little too pleased. Repeating 'my thanks' is warm, slightly flustered.

harlan.pell.pace: explodes on the name, then hard and fast
harlan.pell.wants: to see Pell punished in public
harlan.pell.notes: First 'Pell' disbelieving, the second a shout. The midsummer handshake is bitter memory; 'as a friend' is spat. Ends with a merchant's iron resolve, not tears.

harlan.be.pace: long hesitation, then confesses the cargo, guards the buyer
harlan.be.wants: to admit the cargo while hiding the buyer
harlan.be.notes: The opening pause is him deciding how much to say. He gives the crates and the gold readily and shuts like a till on 'I won't name'. The last line is a deflecting joke that is not funny; he knows exactly whose hole.

harlan.g.wants: to end this line of questions
harlan.g.notes: A practised merchant quip with a smile that doesn't reach the eyes; then he changes the subject a beat too fast. 'Only I've stock to count' is a door closing.

harlan.knew.pace: defensive laugh, repeat, then a quiet confession
harlan.knew.wants: to protect Jory, even at his own cost
harlan.knew.notes: Starts with a fond, dismissive joke; the pause and the repeated 'He didn't know' are him hearing what it means. 'I did.' is barely spoken, almost to himself: the crack in him.

harlan.betrayed.1.wants: to keep his word and be rid of the survivor
harlan.betrayed.1.notes: He keeps the bargain because Jory is home, and that is the only warmth here. The pause is the coins being counted out, not pushed across. 'For the boy' is soft; 'get away from my stall' is flat and final.

harlan.betrayed.2.wants: to be rid of a thief
harlan.betrayed.2.notes: No patter, no 'friend'. Three short blows; the second sentence is an accusation said quietly.

harlan.ash.pace: frantic questions, break, then dead flat
harlan.ash.wants: to know and not know how Jory died
harlan.ash.notes: He asks for the worst detail and then cannot bear the answer; the pauses are him stopping himself. 'There's nothing to bury' is the bottom: quiet, very flat, no crying left in it. Grief and blame at once.

harlan.cb_exposed_pell.wants: to thank the survivor without falling apart
harlan.cb_exposed_pell.notes: Bitter at himself for drinking Pell's wine. Pause before the family line; 'I think' is a dry, queasy half-laugh. He is also relieved the book points at Pell and not at him.

harlan.cb_sold_dig.pace: light, then a bitter little turn
harlan.cb_sold_dig.wants: to deflect judgement by sharing it
harlan.cb_sold_dig.notes: A rueful merchant's shrug; the pause before 'Well' is him recognising himself. 'I've sold worse, to worse' is closer to a confession than he means; covers it with a smile on 'friend'.

harlan.cb_killed_greymuzzle.wants: to keep his grievance against the wolves
harlan.cb_killed_greymuzzle.notes: He admits the wolves didn't take the wagons, then refuses to soften. The wolves were his comfortable story; letting them go means looking at the real one, so the last line is stubborn.

harlan.say_calling.1.wants: to hire a good guard for Jory's future
harlan.say_calling.1.notes: Merchant compliment, genuine. 'If Jory—' breaks on the name and he restarts 'when this is over' a beat too fast, refusing the 'if'.

harlan.say_calling.2.notes: Quick approval of the survivor's size, then the grief turns hard: permission for violence, said low and unsmiling.

harlan.say_calling.3.wants: to find any use for magic in finding Jory
harlan.say_calling.3.notes: Salesman's delight at a novelty; the hope in 'Can it find a lost wagon?' is real. Pause after 'No?' then the joke goes sour.

harlan.say_calling.4.notes: A compliment that slides into Jory without his meaning it to; 'somewhere quiet' sounds like a grave and he hears it. Pause, then the apology, embarrassed.

harlan.say_calling.5.wants: to stop thinking of the boy
harlan.say_calling.5.notes: Starts as idle shop talk; 'My nephew's somewhere quiet' comes out unbidden and sits too long. The apology is tired, not polished.

harlan.jory_now.1.pace: plain, pause, slow, breaks on the last line
harlan.jory_now.1.wants: to be judged for the lie, not pitied
harlan.jory_now.1.notes: The pause is him looking at his own hands. 'First time in his life' is the wound. 'He always did', past tense: Jory's trust is gone and he knows it; let it barely be voiced.

harlan.jory_now.2.pace: affectionate list, then soft and slower
harlan.jory_now.2.wants: to be honest about one thing, at least
harlan.jory_now.2.notes: Starts as a proud uncle's update with a laugh on 'like a horse'. The crates bring the guilt in: the trust is the punishment. Repeated last line, the second quieter.

harlan.t_harlan.pace: slow, storytelling, smile in the voice
harlan.t_harlan.wants: to have the survivor love the boy as he does
harlan.t_harlan.notes: The one unguarded story; his sister's death said simply, the fever year not dwelt on. Warm laugh at 'Do you have a horse?'. Pause before 'I had six', then fond and quiet.

harlan.roost.pace: slow, stops, describes, stops, then urgent
harlan.roost.wants: to get Jory out at any price
harlan.roost.notes: He sits down, which he never does. Two stopped sentences: counting on his fingers, then 'a mouth on him that'll get him—' killed before he says 'killed'. 'Get him out' is the turn into money, the only power he has.

harlan.ledger_early.pace: reading aloud, quickening, pause, then a low plea
harlan.ledger_early.wants: to know who 'R.' is without being the one who acts
harlan.ledger_early.notes: Reads the entries like a merchant checking stock until the date hits. The pause is him looking up. 'If I knew, I'd do something I'd hang for' is quiet and true; he also fears what any inquiry into those crates would show.

harlan.crates.wants: to recover the crates before anyone asks what's in them
harlan.crates.notes: His face falls on 'B.E.'; the first words are flat and careful. Pause while he reaches for paper. 'Paid for is paid for' is a merchant's cover for panic; say it too smoothly.

harlan.be_dig.pace: very long pause, measured patter, too-quick exit
harlan.be_dig.wants: to not admit he sells to the Dig
harlan.be_dig.notes: The silence before speaking is the tell. The salt-and-iron line is a rehearsed justification said evenly; the pause before 'Is there anything else?' and then the subject changes a beat too fast.

harlan.cb_jory_knows.wants: to make the survivor feel what they did
harlan.cb_jory_knows.notes: Opens cold with no good morning. 'You told him' is an accusation, quiet. The last two fragments admit he never would have; let 'any more' fade.

pell.first.wants: to learn what the stranger is worth
pell.first.notes: Soft, smiling self-introduction, every word placed. The 'Terrible' repeated is condolence by rote; the second is a hair too pleased with itself, though he must not sound villainous.

pell.hub.1.pace: a fraction too quick, then over-precise
pell.hub.1.wants: to keep the survivor at a polite distance
pell.hub.1.notes: He is frightened of this person, so he is more polite, not less. The smile comes too quickly; lean on 'specifically', as if pinning them to the business at hand.

pell.hub.2.wants: to open a negotiation on his terms
pell.hub.2.notes: A courteous little joke at his own reputation; the third option is the one he thinks most likely and he is mildly flattered by it.

pell.caravan.pace: gentle, sympathetic, a sting at the end
pell.caravan.wants: to sound sorry while staking a claim
pell.caravan.notes: Condolence in ledger language; 'one hears' distances him from it. 'As a friend' is the tell. The last sentence is the real Pell: a dig at the B.E. crates, said lightly, which he should not have said.

pell.smell.pace: pause, cool warning, then low and confiding
pell.smell.notes: The pause is genuine fright, smoothed over at once. 'Gets said once' is the closest he comes to a threat and it must not sound like one. Drops his voice on the offer; 'Only not do certain other things' is velvet.

pell.confront.1.pace: breaks off, works it out, pause, then smooth again
pell.confront.1.wants: to get the book into the fire
pell.confront.1.notes: The dash is genuine shock. He studies the survivor's face and relaxes when he sees they don't understand; 'How refreshing' is relief as condescension. 'Let's be civilised' is him regaining the ledger voice.

pell.confront.2.notes: No pause for relief this time: he recovers by pure manners. The more frightened he is, the more courteous; 'a good deal of gold' is soft and careful.

pell.why.notes: For once he isn't selling; he hints at the crates without naming them. Pause before the self-portrait, then 'I'm not a good man. I'm a careful one' plainly, with a little dry pride. Ashford sits under it, unsaid.

pell.bribe.notes: A figure and a condition, nothing more. Quiet, very polite, and he is holding his breath.

pell.dig.notes: 'Is it? Go on' is a merchant leaning in. The pause is him working it out. 'Oh, that is worth something' with real pleasure. The arithmetic of the split is smooth; 'Especially me' is a little cat-smile, honest about his appetite.

pell.dig_done.notes: Pleasant, almost genial; the weather line is a wink, said under the breath.

pell.books.pace: breezy list, pause, then low and pointed
pell.books.wants: to share the weight of what he knows
pell.books.notes: Starts as a bored inventory. After the pause he drops the act: the hill is what frightens him. 'I do. I have the receipts' is quiet and precise; the last line is not a joke.

pell.books2.wants: to stop short of what the numbers mean
pell.books2.notes: He retreats into his trade as a shield. 'It's expensive' carries the dread: he means the cost will be paid in lives.

pell.ally.notes: Said without looking at them; 'please' is a courtesy and a warning.

pell.cb_tricked_redcowl.pace: measured, a pause before the last word
pell.cb_tricked_redcowl.wants: to show he noticed and is impressed
pell.cb_tricked_redcowl.notes: He is pleased and also a little afraid of someone who can do that. The ellipsis is him choosing a polite word; 'efficient' is praise in ledger terms.

pell.say_calling.1.wants: to know who the survivor's patron is
pell.say_calling.1.notes: He prices the armour by eye. The second sentence is a genuine fishing line; he can't help asking who paid.

pell.say_calling.2.wants: to defuse the threat by joking about it
pell.say_calling.2.notes: The joke covers real fear of violence; he gets more polite as he says it. 'So simple' is slightly too smooth.

pell.say_calling.3.wants: to flatter while admitting a loss
pell.say_calling.3.notes: A factor's anecdote; the punchline 'You people read the labels' is admiring and a touch irritated.

pell.say_calling.4.notes: He was caught off guard and dislikes it. 'I'll remember it' is a polite note in a ledger, not a threat anyone could repeat to the Watch.

pell.say_calling.5.wants: to reassert control after being surprised
pell.say_calling.5.notes: He didn't notice them arrive, which frightens him. Keep the voice soft and courteous; the chill is in the precision of 'I'll remember it'.

pell.say_woman.wants: to goad a harder bargain he can enjoy
pell.say_woman.notes: Condescending charm that half knows it is condescending. The last clause is self-mocking; smile on 'so rare'.

pell.cb_bribed_snib.wants: to remind the survivor he is the better broker
pell.cb_bribed_snib.notes: Amused at the pump, mildly offended at being cut out. 'And kept it quieter' is the real complaint.

pell.t_pell.pace: precise and even, pauses, almost breaks, recovers
pell.t_pell.wants: to explain himself without being pitied
pell.t_pell.notes: The only time he talks about his sister. The pause is him straightening a pen that was already straight. The boots letter is said plainly, as data; 'She had a dreadful sense of humour' is fond and nearly cracks. The last line goes back to ledger voice.

rav.first.1.pace: lazy, lilting, a grin in it
rav.first.1.wants: to welcome one of his own
rav.first.1.notes: Half-drunk music from the first 'Well, well'. Recognises an outcast and likes them. The titles are a running joke; 'McBreathless' is a mock-posh dodge, said with a wink.

rav.first.2.wants: to get the red cloth out of sight
rav.first.2.notes: He clocks the colours with a smile but the worry is real: red in daylight could hang someone. 'Sit, before Holloway sees you' is kind, said quickly and low.

rav.first.3.wants: to be left in peace, then to be good company
rav.first.3.notes: Starts irritable; the pause is him giving in. Rattles off his history as a joke so nobody asks the real version; 'Ask me which paid better' with a sidelong grin.

rav.hub.1.notes: Two words of real welcome; the trust shows in how little he says.

rav.hub.2.notes: Night-time Rav, a few cups in. Patter with a gag on 'I checked'; the Sella line is frank and unembarrassed, a doctor's matter-of-factness about bodies and noise.

rav.hub.3.wants: to be useful at no cost
rav.hub.3.notes: A barroom aphorism, the punchline on 'and worth it' with a shrug in the voice.

rav.kerchiefs.wants: to keep the survivor alive without saying how he knows
rav.kerchiefs.notes: He knows Redcowl far too well and the first line shows it, with an odd tenderness. Instructions said like a doctor's: clear, unfussed. The joke at the end is a warning.

rav.clerk.1.pace: gossip's lilt, a little too detailed, then quieter
rav.clerk.1.wants: to point the survivor at Jessop and away from himself
rav.clerk.1.notes: He took that key himself, so the frog anecdote is a shade too vivid and too fond. Pause before 'Not seen him since'; that worry is real. The last line is a sad joke.

rav.clerk.2.wants: to share enough and no more
rav.clerk.2.notes: Tells the round story with relish, then 'Draw your own lines, pal' is him stepping back. Pause; the last line arrives as if he has only just noticed, a faint unease.

rav.fence.pace: mock dismay, then business, then a wry warning
rav.fence.notes: 'Oh, dear' is theatrical. He knows a fence and doesn't pretend otherwise. The last sentence is the doctor's frankness: consequences come. A little rueful; he means himself too.

rav.roost.pace: brisk, then a grin, then dry
rav.roost.wants: to get the survivor in safely and keep his own hands clean
rav.roost.notes: The password is a joke between brothers, though he will never say so; let a private smile through on 'owes Rav a leg'. 'I was never here' is said lightly and meant.

rav.redcowl.pace: storytelling roll, stops, pause, then flat
rav.redcowl.wants: to talk about him without saying what he is
rav.redcowl.notes: The leg story is told with comic relish and real affection. The pause is the door closing; 'family histories' slips out and he hears it, so the last line is flat and final.

rav.cb_tricked_redcowl.notes: Shouts the 'RAN'. A lifetime of brotherly score-settling in 'my whole life', though he won't say why. Generous and loud with the drinks.

rav.cb_killed_redcowl.pace: very slow, long pauses, the name almost whispered
rav.cb_killed_redcowl.notes: The one time he names his brother: 'Dunstan' after a long silence, said gently. 'Our mother's idea' is the family reach for mother. The pause is him drinking. 'It was the job' is a brother's bitterness and love. The last two lines are bedside calm turned on himself.

rav.cb_burned_roost.pace: flat report, pause, insistent, then quiet
rav.cb_burned_roost.notes: Says 'He'll have got out' twice in different words, insisting; never names who. The last line drops: the doctor counting the dead in the cages.

rav.cb_exposed_pell.notes: Pure barroom glee; the gag on 'twice' lands with a cup raised.

rav.say_calling.1.wants: to read the survivor like a patient
rav.say_calling.1.notes: A doctor's eye; 'Holloway'd love you' is affectionate and 'don't let him' is real advice from an old Kerchief.

rav.say_calling.2.notes: A doctor's quip delivered without a smile; the joke is in the flatness.

rav.say_calling.3.notes: Prescribes like a GP; the last clause is fond, knowing resignation.

rav.say_calling.4.notes: Light observation, then 'Old Kerchief habit' has a weight on it; the question is friendly and wants an answer: whoever taught them might be someone he knows.

rav.say_calling.5.wants: to place the survivor among the Kerchiefs
rav.say_calling.5.notes: He notices like a doctor and asks like a man who still sends word to the Roost. Keep it friendly; the question is not idle.

rav.say_sella.1.notes: Leaning in; affectionate about Sella's game. 'Notice.' is a dry, single-word instruction.

rav.say_sella.2.wants: to share a joke man to man
rav.say_sella.2.notes: A frank barroom joke about sex and money; slow the delivery on 'She just says it slower' to make the point.

rav.t_rav.pace: lilting, a list that darkens, then a shrug
rav.t_rav.wants: to explain why he stays without saying who he misses
rav.t_rav.notes: He does think of going back; the missing is for his brother, unsaid. The list is funny and grim; the teeth story is the shudder. 'I have a fifth' is the drink as answer.

rav.pain.pace: quick, mock-scolding, then warm and low
rav.pain.wants: to look after them, and maybe more
rav.pain.notes: Doctor's frankness with a flirt under it. 'Don't point' is a laughing hush. 'Largely professionally' is the wink; the anaesthetic gag is self-mocking. Adult, easy, not sleazy.

chid.first.1.wants: to welcome someone carrying the Order's light
chid.first.1.notes: The voice catches on 'Lit!' as if he had stopped hoping years ago. Busy, fussing warmth on 'sit, sit'; 'It used to work' lands lightly, a joke he has told himself a very long time.

chid.first.2.pace: quick, chatty, a small drop at the end
chid.first.2.wants: to make a stranger feel at home
chid.first.2.notes: Pleased just to have a visitor. 'Which is fair' is cheerful, not self-pitying; let 'It used to work' fall half a tone, the only shadow in it.

chid.hub.1.wants: to share good news again with someone who made it possible
chid.hub.1.notes: He checks every morning and is still astonished. The second 'Still burning' is quieter, almost to himself, like a prayer of thanks.

chid.hub.2.wants: to keep hoping without making a fuss
chid.hub.2.notes: Warm greeting, then a gentle self-mocking turn on 'I'm trying to be'. Not sad; a man who has waited a long time and finds that funny.

chid.woke.1.pace: quick start, slowing on the flame
chid.woke.1.wants: to comfort them without telling them what happened
chid.woke.1.notes: Joy on 'You're awake!', then the pause after 'the flame...' is him choosing not to say it was more than the flame. Drop to grave quiet on 'They always keep something': he has seen this before, long ago.

chid.woke.2.wants: to reassure them and not look too closely at how
chid.woke.2.notes: He is not sure what he did and does not want to think about it. The '...well.' is a shrug over something uncanny; keep it light and kind.

chid.where.wants: to make sure they go back carefully
chid.where.notes: Less breathless here; he is telling it straight. 'It knows your smell now' is quiet and practical, an old man's warning more than a boy's fright.

chid.before.pace: slow, halting, long pause before 'It's been a long time'
chid.before.wants: to tell the truth gently without naming it
chid.before.notes: The turn is 'Properly cold, the way the dead go cold': plain, unafraid. 'It's been a long time since I saw anyone do that' is far older than he sounds and he does not notice. Soften 'Rest, now' to a near-whisper.

chid.shrine.pace: rambling, building to the comic beat
chid.shrine.wants: to explain the flame without sounding as lost as he feels
chid.shrine.notes: 'Kept the dead lying down' is said simply, as fact. The list of attempts gathers speed and comedy; 'That was a bad day' is a dry little wince.

chid.relight.wants: to let the old rite work without fuss
chid.relight.notes: Say the childhood words simply, as remembered. A breath before the kettle line, which is gently funny, not played for a laugh.

chid.lit.wants: to tell the whole world at once
chid.lit.notes: The voice cracks on 'WORKS' with years of vindication. Climb through 'I said it worked!'; the final 'Oh, thank you!' should catch, close to tears.

chid.blessed.wants: to send them off held and safe
chid.blessed.notes: A blessing given as easily as handing over a coat. Low and close; 'be warm' carries real priestly weight under the plainness.

chid.warden.pace: thoughtful, wandering, a beat before the last clause
chid.warden.wants: to answer honestly without saying how he knows
chid.warden.notes: 'Before me, certainly, which is a long time' slips out too old; don't mark it. The last line about guards turning on us lands quietly, as if he means himself and the survivor.

chid.vault.pace: plain, unhurried, a beat before the last line
chid.vault.wants: to point them at the truth without betraying Vonnra
chid.vault.notes: The fool lets the theologian through: 'That, I think, is the answer' is calm and quietly sharp. No gossip in it.

chid.below.wants: to admit a fear he has carried for a long time
chid.below.notes: 'Digging. Down.' as two separate thoughts. The Order's saying is recited with old familiarity; 'It sounds like a threat' is light on the surface, uneasy underneath.

chid.long.pace: cheerful, then a stumble, then too quick
chid.long.wants: to change the subject before the number comes out
chid.long.notes: Catch on 'Since— well.' as he nearly says a date. Real fondness on Rook's mother and the bread; the candle line is a bolt for the exit, bright and unconvincing.

chid.cb_opened_vault.wants: to know and not to know at the same time
chid.cb_opened_vault.notes: Delight and terror in the same breath. Each 'No'/'Yes' flips hard; the last 'No.' is small and sure, because he already knows what is down there.

chid.cb_vault2.pace: slow, then quicker on the candles
chid.cb_vault2.wants: to believe the old dead are still doing their job
chid.cb_vault2.notes: 'Good, I think' is honest doubt. The candle line is a frightened man doing the one thing he can, with a wobble of humour on top.

chid.cb_core_stolen.wants: to take in a disaster quietly
chid.cb_core_stolen.notes: The repeated 'Oh, dear' grows smaller, not louder. 'One of the old ones' is said like someone who knew it when it was new; 'carried about' is almost comic in its understatement.

chid.cb_nemesis_slain.wants: to celebrate and look after them
chid.cb_nemesis_slain.notes: Answers his own question before they can: 'It was horrible' is pure sympathy. Mother-hen bustle on 'Not there. There.', bright and bossy.

chid.say_calling.1.pace: quick, with a small pause at 'dents'
chid.say_calling.1.wants: to praise the shield for what it has survived
chid.say_calling.1.notes: Pleased by the memory of the knights, as if he saw them. 'Dents mean it worked' is warm and a touch proud of them.

chid.say_calling.2.wants: to tell them they are not too much for the light
chid.say_calling.2.notes: No judgement at all; a priest's ease. 'Fire with manners' is a little joke offered as comfort, smiled through.

chid.say_calling.3.wants: to look at what they are without frightening them
chid.say_calling.3.notes: The halt on 'oh. Like you.' is recognition: he knows exactly what that burning is. Recover into a fluster on 'Sorry'; 'I won't, but I'll try' is candid and fond.

chid.say_calling.4.wants: to tease them for creeping up on him
chid.say_calling.4.notes: Unbothered, amused. The spiders line is a cheerful non sequitur; play it straight and it gets the laugh.

chid.say_calling.5.wants: to make a joke of being startled
chid.say_calling.5.notes: Same text as the stalker variant, for any other calling: a little startled, then pleased with his own joke about the spiders. Keep it brisk.

chid.names.pace: slow, pauses after the question and after 'I saw you think'
chid.names.wants: to warn them before they lose what he has lost
chid.names.notes: The real old man speaks here. He watches them struggle for the name and recognises it from inside; 'It always takes the names first' is experience, not theory. Then the apology and 'Sit, sit' pull back into the fool, too quickly.

chid.t_chid.pace: bright and loud to start, then slow and quiet
chid.t_chid.wants: to remember them out loud for a moment
chid.t_chid.notes: Big happy memory on 'Loud!' and Brother Aumery, the voice catching on joy. Long pause before 'They're all gone now'; 'I keep not' is barely above a breath. He was there.

chid.note.pace: quick and bright, a hard stop at 'Cormac, once, who—'
chid.note.wants: to steer away from his own handwriting
chid.note.notes: He wrote the note. The list of C-names is a babble to fill the air; stop dead mid-memory at Cormac. 'In... well. Ages.' trails off as he hears himself nearly say how long.

chid.cb_nell.wants: to tell them gently that it is done
chid.cb_nell.notes: He is quiet, which he never is: keep it low and unadorned. 'Of course, iron' knows exactly what Brannoc's iron means. 'She was very light' is the hardest line; then the old fussing about where to sit, softer than usual.

vonnra.first.1.pace: very slow, long pauses between sentences
vonnra.first.1.wants: to place the stranger and set the terms
vonnra.first.1.notes: She has heard about this one already and lets it pass for a glance. Weight on 'The toll is the toll'. A faint, dry pleasure on 'You, of all people': a reader will want answers she will not give.

vonnra.first.2.pace: slow, a long held pause after 'ford'
vonnra.first.2.wants: to look at what she made without showing it
vonnra.first.2.notes: She has waited for this one. The pause before 'Sooner than I had thought' is the only crack, the closest she comes to pleasure; then back to the toll as if nothing was said. No contractions, no hurry.

vonnra.first.3.wants: to establish who holds the gate
vonnra.first.3.notes: Flat, final terms. 'I remember your face' is not a threat so much as a statement of fact. Keep the alto low with a little air; give nothing away.

vonnra.hub.1.pace: very slow, a long pause before 'Payment, always'
vonnra.hub.1.wants: to keep the arrangement while conceding nothing
vonnra.hub.1.notes: After the accusation she now uses their name, and that is her only answer: say it quietly, as if it costs something. 'The next one is not' is a warning and an invitation at once.

vonnra.hub.2.wants: to close the chapter and keep the door open
vonnra.hub.2.notes: Plain and still. 'Payment, always' is her refrain; let it sound like policy, not greed.

vonnra.hub.3.pace: very slow, distant, almost to herself
vonnra.hub.3.wants: to keep watch on the ford
vonnra.hub.3.notes: She is looking south toward the crossing and does not turn. 'It will not always be' comes from someone who knows exactly what is coming, because she arranged it.

vonnra.hub.4.wants: to talk business and nothing else
vonnra.hub.4.notes: Mild contempt for disorder. A merchant's remark on the surface; underneath, she is pleased Coyle's wagons are not reaching the Dig.

vonnra.hub.5.wants: to remind them the terms have not changed
vonnra.hub.5.notes: Two words, all patience. Not cold; final.

vonnra.paid.pace: slow, a beat before the second sentence
vonnra.paid.wants: to send them through and keep them
vonnra.paid.notes: 'Try to come back through it' sounds like courtesy; it is an investment she means to protect. A thread of warmth she would deny.

vonnra.ledger.wants: to put a price on the truth
vonnra.ledger.notes: A clean refusal dressed as a fee. No defensiveness, though the ledger holds more than she lets on.

vonnra.ledger_read.wants: to point them away from her own gate
vonnra.ledger_read.notes: Every sentence is true and chosen. 'Whatever happened to it' is said with perfect calm about a thing her clerk did and she allowed.

vonnra.vault.pace: very slow, long pause before the second sentence
vonnra.vault.wants: to shut the door on the one subject she cannot sell
vonnra.vault.notes: The only time she gives anything for nothing, and it is a no without saying no. Lower and harder than usual; let the stillness carry the weight.

vonnra.arcana.wants: to warn a reader off without explaining
vonnra.arcana.notes: Recognition that this one can read the door. Pronounce the Latin cleanly, as someone who knows it well. 'Ask me something cheaper' is dry, almost amused, and firmly closing.

vonnra.ford.pace: very slow, long pause before 'It is not often'
vonnra.ford.wants: to remember the night it worked
vonnra.ford.notes: She is describing what she watched for, not saw by magic. 'It is not often the second thing happens' is the nearest she comes to awe; then she recovers into the fee, and waives it, because she is pleased.

vonnra.fortune.pace: slow, deliberate, a held breath before the last sentence
vonnra.fortune.wants: to read the result of her own work
vonnra.fortune.notes: Practical and exact about the hand. 'I have been waiting to see how it came out' is literal, and she lets it sound like ordinary curiosity.

vonnra.f_beasts.1.wants: to make them feel the broken promise
vonnra.f_beasts.1.notes: The image of the old wolf is tender; the blood is not. 'So will I' is quiet and final, the closest she comes to a reproach.

vonnra.f_beasts.2.wants: to mark the one choice she respects
vonnra.f_beasts.2.notes: The clear water is said with real pleasure. 'Most people never learn the difference' is approval from someone who rarely gives it.

vonnra.f_beasts.3.wants: to warn them about what they lead
vonnra.f_beasts.3.notes: Interest in the image of wolves at their side; the Holloway line is reported gossip, said as sight. The last sentence is a caution from someone who also leads things where she wants them.

vonnra.f_beasts.4.wants: to show them the cost plainly
vonnra.f_beasts.4.notes: Pelts said without colour. The final sentence is clinical, a ledger entry of extinction; no anger, only distance.

vonnra.f_beasts.5.pace: slow, a pause before the simile
vonnra.f_beasts.5.wants: to name the price of their safety
vonnra.f_beasts.5.notes: 'Too quiet' is a small verdict. The fire simile lands softly and stays.

vonnra.f_beasts.6.wants: to show them what happened while they looked away
vonnra.f_beasts.6.notes: The Watchman's death is reported, not mourned. 'The world was not' is cool and exact.

vonnra.f_beasts.7.pace: slow, measured, a pause before Wenna
vonnra.f_beasts.7.wants: to show them they are part of the trade now
vonnra.f_beasts.7.notes: Some kinship in 'Someone always is': she is in the business of payment too. The Wenna line drops into something more serious; Wenna is a watcher she respects.

vonnra.f_beasts.8.notes: 'Dimly' is a seer's word for 'nobody has told me yet'. Calm, with no reproach.

vonnra.f_caravan.1.pace: slow, long pause before the last sentence
vonnra.f_caravan.1.wants: to show them what their truth did to a family
vonnra.f_caravan.1.notes: Jory's knowledge came from Jory's lips to someone who sold it on. The last sentence is quiet and heavy; she knows exactly what the uncle carried and why.

vonnra.f_caravan.2.pace: slow, even, warmer at the end
vonnra.f_caravan.2.notes: A plain good outcome, given its due. 'At every table it sits at' carries a faint irony about Coyle tables.

vonnra.f_caravan.3.wants: to warn them that secrets travel
vonnra.f_caravan.3.notes: Spoken by a woman whose trade is the travelling of secrets. A thin edge, not a threat.

vonnra.f_caravan.4.wants: to note what they saved and what they let go
vonnra.f_caravan.4.notes: 'Thinner than when they left' is exact, unpitying. The last sentence closes the door on the rest.

vonnra.f_caravan.5.wants: to let them carry it themselves
vonnra.f_caravan.5.notes: The refusal to describe is the mercy and the judgement. 'You know.' is two quiet words, nothing added.

vonnra.f_caravan.6.wants: to remind them the work is unfinished
vonnra.f_caravan.6.notes: 'Neither are you' has a double weight she alone understands: she has plans for them. Keep it level.

vonnra.f_pell.1.wants: to let them see a schemer caught in his own trap
vonnra.f_pell.1.notes: 'Built for someone else' carries the cut. 'It is all he has left to do' has a sliver of pity, the kind one keeper of accounts feels for another.

vonnra.f_pell.2.pace: slow, a measured beat before 'They are not in this town'
vonnra.f_pell.2.wants: to hint at the reach of Pell's connections
vonnra.f_pell.2.notes: The repeated 'Pell' is faintly mocking. The last sentence is a warning lightly dressed as gossip.

vonnra.f_pell.3.wants: to remind them they are now in someone's books
vonnra.f_pell.3.notes: She knows what it is to have names in a ledger; she has bought plenty. 'I would keep an eye on all of them' is genuine advice, and includes herself.

vonnra.f_pell.4.pace: slow, a long rolling sentence then a short one
vonnra.f_pell.4.wants: to warn them of a grudge travelling south
vonnra.f_pell.4.notes: The fast horse is said with the stillness of someone who never runs. Last line flat and certain, not dramatic.

vonnra.f_pell.5.pace: slow, the last sentence slower still
vonnra.f_pell.5.wants: to warn them they are on someone's tally
vonnra.f_pell.5.notes: Two counters regarding each other. 'One day he will count you' is gentle and chilling; she is counting them already.

vonnra.f_self.1.pace: very slow, long pause before 'and I would very much'
vonnra.f_self.1.wants: to watch their face while pretending not to know
vonnra.f_self.1.notes: She knows exactly what did not want them to stay down: she did. Say 'I would very much like to know what' with perfect, mild sincerity; the lie must be invisible.

vonnra.f_self.2.pace: slow, a beat before the last sentence
vonnra.f_self.2.notes: Her one near-joke. Bone-dry; no smile in the voice, only in the word 'flattering'.

vonnra.f_self.3.wants: to tell them what the town now thinks of them
vonnra.f_self.3.notes: The contrast between dogs and people is quietly pointed. A small, cool pleasure in the phrasing.

vonnra.f_self.4.pace: very slow, long pause after 'lit for you'
vonnra.f_self.4.wants: to admire her work without claiming it
vonnra.f_self.4.notes: She lit those lamps herself. 'They have not done that for anyone in a long time' carries a hush close to tenderness; she must not sound like she is confessing.

vonnra.f_below.1.pace: slow, building, trailing at the end
vonnra.f_below.1.wants: to show them the shape of what is coming
vonnra.f_below.1.notes: The fullest picture she gives; she knows it all from lore and reports. Contempt-tinged pity for the lamp-people on 'grateful'. Trail off on 'the door in the hillside...' and leave it hanging.

vonnra.f_below.2.pace: slow, deliberate, trailing at the end
vonnra.f_below.2.notes: As the longer reading, without the farm. Weight on 'grateful', with a sliver of pity; leave the door hanging unfinished.

vonnra.f_door.1.pace: very slow, the name given its own pause
vonnra.f_door.1.wants: to keep them close now that they know
